concepts.gloss: A written device indicating grammatical structure or meaning, covering marks, spaces and typographic changes.
A writing indicator occupying its own linear position in a sequence of written symbols.
A segmental symbol used to signal structural or interpretative properties in written text.
A segmental space separating orthographic words.
A modification of existing written letter forms used for structural or interpretative signalling.
Change from the default lower-case roman type to capital, italic, bold or small-capital form.
Use of a capital at the start of an ordinary written sentence as a non-segmental indicator.
Use of a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark as a terminal sentence-boundary indicator.
Punctuation placed within written word forms, typically hyphens and apostrophes.
Accent or other mark usually belonging to spelling rather than to punctuation.
Punctuation such as paired quotes and parentheses that can span multiple sentences.
Break in text signalled by a new line and usually indentation, counted as punctuation.
Exclusion of chapter, section and hierarchical heading layout from the punctuation domain.

rules.statement: Punctuation indicators are written devices that give cues to grammatical structure or meaning, including marks, spaces and eligible changes of typography.
rules.condition: For a stretch of written text, identify a punctuation indicator by the grammatical or interpretive cue it supplies, not simply by whether it is a separate printed symbol.

contrast.text: The note ends 'The lane is clear.' [full stop is an indicator]
A sentence starts 'Tomorrow we leave.' [initial capital is an indicator]
The invented novel title Winter Harbour is printed in italics. [type style marks a title]
The phrase 'Well, we tried' contains a comma. [structural cue]

rules.statement: Segmental punctuation indicators take up distinct positions in written linear sequences; the category comprises punctuation marks and word spaces.
rules.condition: Identify a written mark or word-separating blank as segmental when it occupies an independent place in the string, as opposed to changing the presentation of a letter.

contrast.text: Rain fell, then stopped. [comma is a segmental mark]
The sequence 'blue ribbon' includes a segmental word space.
Is the bridge open? [terminal question mark]
The two words 'three chairs' are separated by a word space.

rules.statement: Non-segmental punctuation modifies existing written symbols through features such as capitalisation, italics, bold face or small capitals when they serve a punctuation-related purpose.
rules.condition: When a change of case or type style conveys sentence beginning, quotation, title or emphasis, classify the change as a non-segmental punctuation modification rather than as another written segment.

exceptions.description: Type styling used solely to show larger heading or chapter hierarchy is outside this definition of punctuation.

rules.statement: In ordinary writing sentence beginnings are indicated non-segmentally through an initial capital, while sentence endings are marked segmentally by a full stop, question mark or exclamation mark.
rules.condition: For a typical orthographic sentence in running text, distinguish the initial capital-letter change from its terminal punctuation mark; do not infer a universal rule for all fragment and quotation styles.

contrast.text: The parcel arrived. [capital and full stop]
Has the parcel arrived? [capital and question mark]
Watch that step! [capital and exclamation mark]
The line 'The light is on.' begins with a capital and ends with a full stop.

rules.statement: Apostrophes and hyphens are punctuation marks normally placed within orthographic words, unlike most marks delimiting expressions or sentences.
rules.condition: When analysing punctuation inside a written word, classify apostrophes and hyphens as the normal word-internal marks, while distinguishing them from commas and sentence terminal marks.

contrast.text: Mira's notebook was missing. [word-internal apostrophe]
The pre-owned machine was checked. [hyphen in a written compound]
The ferry returned, but the captain stayed. [comma between constituents]
The gardeners' tools were locked away. [apostrophe after a plural ending]

rules.concept: diacritics as spelling rather than punctuation
rules.statement: Diacritics on letters are normally aspects of word spelling rather than punctuation, although a diaeresis can have a borderline hyphen-like function in certain American spellings.
rules.condition: For accents and other diacritics in a word, treat them as word-spelling rather than punctuational indicators, except for the borderline use of a diaeresis to mark a vowel break in some AmE forms.

exceptions.description: The diaeresis in AmE coöperate is a borderline case functioning similarly to a hyphen, unlike ordinary accents in word spelling.

contrast.text: She updated her résumé. [accents belong to spelling]
Her fiancé arrived at noon. [accent is not punctuation]
The research groups agreed to coöperate. [AmE diaeresis with hyphen-like function]
The editor instead printed co-operate with a hyphen.

rules.statement: Punctuation may operate above sentence level: quotation marks and parentheses can enclose several sentences, and paragraph breaks may be indicated by a new line and usually indentation.
rules.condition: When punctuation encloses writing longer than one sentence, recognise paired quotations or parentheses, or a paragraph division signalled by a new line, as potentially within punctuation's domain.

contrast.text: The notice says: "The gate is open. Use the left lane." [multi-sentence quotation]
An aside reads (The doors are locked. Use the rear path.) [multi-sentence parenthesis]
The editor separates two paragraphs by a new line and indentation. [paragraph division]
A transcript encloses a two-sentence reply in quotation marks. [scope above sentence]

rules.concept: functional boundary between punctuation and document layout
rules.statement: A type-style change can indicate punctuation when it marks a title, quotation or emphasis, but is outside punctuation when it simply conveys the structure of chapters, sections or headings.
rules.condition: Classify use of italics, bold or similar typography according to function: textual meaning or status marking belongs to punctuation, while heading-level or chapter layout organisation is excluded.

exceptions.description: The source excludes chapter/section structure and heading formatting from punctuation even when these use the same typographic devices.

The manual italicises a section heading to mark hierarchy. [document layout]
The chapter titles appear in a larger font to mark organisation. [document layout]
